title: How To Create Garments For Inzoi Using Marvelous Designer Everywear
Description: Learn step by step how to create amazing garments for the InZOI game using Marvelous Designer Everywear! In this video, we ...
Transcript:
Hello everyone. My name is Gabrielle
Bkoi and I'm a specialist in 3D design
and implementation.
In this tutorial, we will show you how
to use Marvelous Designer Everywhere to
create clothes for the game Ino. Let's
go to the video.
The first step is to download the assets
provided in the Connect Store. You'll
find the links in the description below.
Make sure to download the entire folder
and unzip it as it contains several
assets we'll be using through the
process. I like linking my folders in
the library so I can quickly access the
assets whenever I need them. Once you
open the files, you'll notice that both
avatars have red lines along the wrists.
This indicates that the garment's
sleeves should not extend beyond that
point.
For pants, ensure that they do not touch
the ground.
Additionally, the female avatar has a
red area along the hips, which means
skirts should ideally not go below this
line, as doing so makes the rigging
process more challenging.
Here I have a three-piece look that I
prepared specifically to demonstrate
various scenarios and best practices
when preparing a garment for a video
game. Video games generally require
maximum asset optimization. So if you
have a garment that is true to life with
all the patterns, finishes, and details,
we will need to adjust it to ensure
better rigging and optimization inside
the game. Take this cardigan as an
example. It has folded cuffs and hem
just like in real life. To adapt it to
the game, I will cut and remove half of
the patterns.
To add realism to the patterns, we will
use additional thickness rendering. But
first, make sure you are using the thick
textured surface option in the 3D window
toggle menu. I'll start by selecting the
cardigan cuffs and hemline and adding 5
mm of thickness. This creates the effect
of two layers of fabric, which is what I
want.
I'll do the same for the placket.
Next, I'll hide the cardigan to work on
the bodysuit. Since this piece won't be
very visible, I don't need to worry too
much about the arm holes. However, if I
wanted to use this garment without the
jacket in in later, I would recommend
increasing its additional thickness
rendering to 3 mm. I'll apply the same
logic to the shorts. increasing the
thickness of patterns that represent
double layers or that are generally
thicker.
Now I'll bring the cardigan back. Before
moving on to everywhere, there's one
more quick step. Since my file is
currently in high resolution, I will
increase the particle distance to 8 and
change the additional thickness
collision to 2.5 mm to ensure the
garment remains stable during
simulation.
Finally, I'll activate the wireframe so
you can see the mesh. For better rigging
results, it's ideal to have a quad mesh.
Fortunately, Marvelous has a special
algorithm that converts the mesh to
quads while keeping it optimized and
respecting the garment's curvature. So,
I'll select all the patterns with Ctrl
A. Then, I will rightclick and change
the mesh type to quad optimized. Before
running the optimization, here's a
useful tip. Reduce the poly count by
adjusting the resolution of the pattern
edges. By default, this value is set to
six. So, I'll select all my patterns and
lower it to two. Since in most areas,
this won't be noticeable.
Next, using the edit pattern tool, I can
manually adjust areas where I want
higher resolution, such as the cardigan
placket, which I'll set to four.
I'll do the same adjustment to some of
the hem lines.
Now, it's time to open everywhere. Start
by selecting connect, then everywhere.
Once the window opens, you'll see the
avatar and garment polygon count
displayed in both the 3D window and in
the everywhere panel. The number we need
to focus on is the garment polygons.
For Enzo, we recommend a maximum of
15,000 quads for looks that contain top
and bottom and 20,000 quads for looks
that contain top, bottom, and outerwear.
Before running the optimization, we
strongly recommend converting all of
your top stitches from OBJ to texture.
Since top stitches account for a
significant portion of the total polygon
count in this project, switching them to
texture will greatly reduce the overall
number of garment polygons.
I'll set my goal to 30,000 quads, which
is is slightly higher than the 20k limit
because I know I'll use other tools
later to reduce it further. Now, click
optimize and marvelous will increase the
particle distance of the garments to
help us reach the target.
If you prefer, instead of using
everywhere optimization, you can
manually adjust the particle distance
for each pattern individually. This
approach give you greater control over
the garment, allowing you to decide
which areas require higher resolution
and where a lower mesh density is
acceptable. When you use everywhere
optimization tool, it transforms all
trims into plain type. Meaning each trim
is now represented by a flat surface
with a texture like you can see here
with this button.
If a trim is close to the avatar's face
and might be seen up close, you may want
to revert it to a mesh type. To do this,
click the trim in the object browser and
uncheck plane. Then manually you can
reduce the poly count. I'll set mine to
500, which should be enough for this
button. For less noticeable trims, like
the belt buckle, I'll leave them as
plain type.
Next, we need to mask out parts that
won't be visible in the game. For
example, the lower and back sections of
the bodysuit will be hidden by the
shorts and cardigan, so we can mask
those out. Click the paintbrush icon to
start masking. I prefer working in the
2D window, but you can also hide parts
in the 3D view. Note that the 2D window
has front and back tabs, so you can
choose which side of the mesh to hide.
Since I want to hide the mesh on both
sides of the fabric, I'll select the
double-sided brush option and then I can
paint the areas of the patterns that I
know will not appear in the game as the
lower part of the bodysuit and the back
pattern.
We can also mess the internal mesh of
patterns to reduce even more the poly
count. I will uncheck the double-sided
brush, switch to back view, and select
enclosed region.
Then I can select the inner mesh of
patterns that won't be visible during
the game play like the sleeves.
Don't mask areas like the shorts hems as
they might be visible from certain
angles.
Once you finish, you can select exit.
As you can see, these steps allowed us
to reduce the poly count while
maintaining the garment's high quality.
Next, we'll use the auto seal tool to
ensure a clean finish in areas that can
be closed. Here, I'll hide my avatar
using the shift A shortcut so we can get
a better view of the garment's internal
part.
Then I can choose between the disk or 3D
pen option. They work very similarly.
With the disk option, imagine you're
sealing the leaf with a circular shape.
You simply need to click on three points
that will define where the disc will be
created. Next, Marvelous will ask you to
pick one of the sides of the mesh you
want to seal. I'll select the bottom
part. And now you can see that it has
sealed the sleeve opening. This
guarantees a cleaner finish when we
bring the avatar back and ensures that
areas without polygons won't be visible
inside during game play. Please note
that the applied auto seal can only be
viewed in the 3D window when using the
thick textured surface mode and any
nonvisible inner mesh of the pattern
will be automatically masked.
Since we won't be simulating cloth
physics in real time, we need to read
the garment so it moves according to the
avatar's movements.
You can start by clicking on apply.
Next, we need to check if the garment
looks correct during different avatar
motions.
Go back to the library and inside the
assets folder, you'll find the motion
folder. Double click it to apply. Then
go to the animation menu and open the
animation editor. First, right click on
the timeline and select clank range to
active frames so we can watch the entire
animation.
Then hit play and analyze whether the
garment behaves correctly.
Here we are looking for parts of the
garment that aren't moving with the
avatar, areas where the mesh is
colliding with the body or other
fabrics, and regions around the joints
that appear unnatural.
After the first animation, we return to
frame one and check the second motion.
This motion will stretch the avatar's
body so we can verify whether the
weights are evenly distributed after
rigging.
We have several other tools that can
assist during the rigging and weight
painting process and you can learn more
about them in our everywhere tutorial
which will be linked in the description
below. As everything looks correct, we
can now click on switch to bind pose and
move on to the next step.
Now we can move to the material tab in
everywhere.
Before clicking pack UVs, I recommend
selecting auto patterns and in your
property editor choosing side face under
UV expansion.
This will ensure that our texture
extends to the sides of the patterns.
I'll also increase the seam size to
eight and then select back UVs.
If you have large patterns that won't
appear in the game, such as the bodysuit
back, you can slightly reduce the size
before running the UV packing. This will
guarantee a higher resolution for
patterns that will actually be visible
in the game. Finally, you can click
exit.
The next step is baking. Click apply
next to baking to generate the maps.
Here we will generate the detailed
normal map and ambient occlusion maps.
They will guarantee a higher resolution
effect in your garment without
compromising the polygon count.
Before moving on, make sure to save a
good thumbnail image of your garment as
it will be used it later on.
Now we can finally click export and type
in our garment's name.
In the export options, make sure you
select Enzo as the platform and choose
thick object. If your garment has any
type of opacity, select the armoal
option.
I would be able to select the arm option
if I hadn't set my buckle trim as a
plane. Since it uses a PNG texture, I
need to go with the armoal option. Now I
can click okay. Just keep in mind before
exporting you need to ensure all your
patterns are rigged and that all your
UVs are packed within a single tile.
Otherwise, you'll see an error message
when you click the export button. One
more step is needed before we can bring
our garment into the game. This will be
done using the mod kit provided by
Enzoy. You can download it using the
link in the description or by searching
for Enzoy Mod Kit in your Epic Games app
and clicking to download it. Once the
download is complete, open the mod kit.
We will start by duplicating an existing
garment to use as the base for our mod.
Select create a Zoy, then change the
drop-down to set. Use the check boxes
for male, female, adult, and youth to
filter assets according to the garment
you created. I recommend choosing the
garment that most closely resembles your
design, as this will make masking body
parts easier later. Since my outfit has
shorts and long sleeves, I'll use this
jumpsuit as the base. Click the arrow
and select create new mod project.
Add a name and description for your mod.
Then click create. A new folder will be
generated for your project. Next, click
the arrow next to your newly created mod
and select open mod workspace. A window
will appear asking if you want to create
a copy of the source asset data. Then
click copy.
Now we will replace the current garment
with our own mesh and textures. Scroll
down and click open resource import
tool. This special window allows you to
import assets in a standardized way.
First ensure skeletal mesh outfit is
selected.
Drag and drop the FBX file exported from
Marvelous and wait for it to load.
Then move on to the textures.
Click the base color button and drag and
drop the base color image.
Repeat this process for the normal arm
and thumbnail images.
After that, close the resource import
tool. You'll notice new folders called
the mesh and texture inside your project
folder. Start by opening the mesh folder
and selecting the garment file you just
imported. Scroll up to where the current
mesh is listed and click the arrow icon
to replace the jumpsuit with the file
you selected in the object browser. Now
we need to add a new material for this
outfit. Start by clicking the MCAS
button and typing the name of your
material.
Click the arrow next to the material to
reveal the slots where we will add our
maps.
Next, go to the textures folder. Select
the arm texture and then click the arrow
to apply this image as the map.
Repeat the same process for the normal
and base [clears throat] color maps.
Now our texture is set, but we still
need to apply it to the garment mesh.
First, click to the folder icon next to
your material.
This will take you to its location
inside the project folder. Then double
click the mesh asset to open its editor.
In the material slot, click the arrow
icon to apply the newly created material
to the mesh.
Finally, save and close this window.
Since I also imported my thumbnail
image, I'll navigate to the textures
folder, select the thumbnail, and apply
it to the thumbnail slot.
We are almost ready. The last step is to
make sure the body regions being masked
out are correct. This is important to
avoid collisions and improve game
performance.
Enzoy uses a group ID system that makes
it easy for users to hide specific body
parts. Under the body hiding section,
you'll see which areas are masked based
on the garment we selected as the base
earlier.
Scroll up and click enable body region
hiding. This option gives you a preview
of the parts that will be hidden during
the game.
Since I started with a jumpsuit, my mask
is already correct. As you can see, the
visible areas of the body display the
colorful texture, which represents the
body masking region guide.
I'll hide the garment preview so you can
see that all body areas covered by the
garment are masked out.
But let's imagine that my garment was a
short sleeve t-shirt. In that case, I
would scroll down and instead of arms
all, I would choose arms all short. So,
the avatar arms would remain visible in
the game. If you need more details about
Inzo's body hiding system, I'll leave a
link in the description with a more
detailed explanation.
Now I return to the original preview
settings.
Then click save and select the arrow to
go back to my projects.
To test the mod on your computer, click
the arrow next to your project and
select create local mod package. Save
the file in the 88849
folder located inside the mods folder in
ISO documents.
The mods will still work within the main
mods folder, but for better management,
we recommend placing them in the 88A49
folder.
Then wait until you see the popup
message, packaging successful.
Now you can launch Inzo. Just make sure
to check if the mods are available. Go
to options, mods, and make sure that
enable mods option is turned on.
Next, enter the character studio. Choose
the avatar type and open the outfit tab.
Go to sets. Scroll down till you find
your outfit and click to wear it.
All your created outfits will have a mod
icon next to them.
Now that we have confirmed our mod is
working properly, we can share it
through the connect game platform. This
allow other players to access your
creations and use them in their own
game. First, navigate to the folder
where we just saved the package file.
Select the folder you want to upload and
compress it into a zip file.
Next, we will upload our garment into
gameware. Start by logging into connect
and clicking the upload button. On the
upload screen, select game wear. Then in
Windows file explorer, select the zip
file of the outfit you want to upload.
Here you can add the name, the
description, tags, and other images to
your file. Then we can set the garment
category for our item. Adding categories
will improve the item compatibility and
search results since users can search
and filter items by category.
In the recolor option, select
unavailable since we haven't created a
RGB mask map that would allow us to
recolor garments inside in Zoy. For
pricing options, the pricing feature is
currently unavailable and only free
items are allowed. Then click publish to
make the item public. You can also click
draft to keep the item hidden from other
users while allowing further editing or
re-uploading.
You can view your uploaded items under
the gameware tab in your profile.
And that's it. We have just finished
creating our Inzo mod using marvelous
designer everywhere tools and gameware.
So you can share your creations with
friends. I hope you enjoyed this
tutorial. See you next time.

title: New Keyframeable Properties In Marvelous Designer 2025.2 Take Animation To The Next Level
Transcript:
Key frame animation now offers more
control over pattern, trim, and tack
properties. To demonstrate, we created a
few animations using the new features.
This robot can self-inflate. To make
that happen, we'll use the first new key
framable property, shrinkage. We'll
increase the shrinkage weft and warp,
expanding both the vertical and
horizontal area of the fabric around the
robot. You can key frame shrinkage to
tighten or loosen fabric during
animation. You can even use this to make
a self-lengthening skirt.
Next up, pressure. By key framing a
pressure increase, our robot inflates.
You can key frame positive and negative
pressure to animate inflation or
deflation. By key framing solidify, you
can modify how stiff or flexible your
fabric is during an animation. We'll use
this to toughen up our robot after it
inflates, causing it to wrinkle less as
it moves. In another example, we
increased the solidity on this shirt
during the jump, causing it to flutter
less and hold its shape better in the
wind. To demonstrate what tack key
frames can do, we'll tack a ball to the
robot's hand. We'll add a key frame that
weakens the tack, causing the ball to
fall to the ground. But don't worry,
we'll give it back to the robot. To do
that, we'll show off the final new key
framable property, trim weight. Since
the ball is a trim, we can key frame its
weight to decrease right as it hits the
ground. Now that the ball is lighter,
the tack pulls it back up to the robot.
Summary: ### Summary of Video on Key Frame Animation Features **Main Topic and Purpose:** The video discusses new features in key frame animation that enhance control over various properties like shrinkage, pressure, solidity, tack, and trim weight. The purpose is to demonstrate these features through practical examples, showcasing how they can be applied in animations. **Content Breakdown:** 1. **Introduction:** - Introduction to new key frame animation capabilities. - Emphasis on improved control over fabric properties in animations. 2. **Key Points:** - **Shrinkage:** - Introduced as a key frame property that allows for the manipulation of fabric dimensions. - Demonstrated by animating a robot that can self-inflate by adjusting shrinkage in both the weft and warp directions, enabling the creation of effects like a self-lengthening skirt. - **Pressure:** - Key framing pressure enables the animation of inflation and deflation. - Example given where increasing pressure causes the robot to inflate, and vice versa. - **Solidify:** - This property adjusts the stiffness or flexibility of the fabric during animations. - Illustrated with a robot that becomes stiffer after inflation, resulting in less wrinkling during movement, and a shirt that maintains shape better in the wind. - **Tack:** - Tack key frames control the adhesion of objects. - Demonstrated by tacking a ball to the robot's hand and then weakening the tack to drop the ball. - **Trim Weight:** - This feature allows for the adjustment of an object's weight within the animation. - The example shows decreasing the weight of the ball as it hits the ground, allowing the tack to pull it back to the robot. 3. **Conclusion:** - The video effectively showcases how these new key frame properties can be utilized to create dynamic and realistic animations, enhancing both the visual appeal and functionality of animated characters and objects. Overall, the video serves as an instructional guide for animators looking to leverage new key frame features to improve their animation techniques.

Description: This short tutorial walks you through the process for creating custom arrangement points and bounding volumes for custom ...
Transcript:
Welcome to a new quick tutorial where we
will talk about how to create custom
arrangement points and bounding volumes
for our custom avatars in Marvel's
designer.
First of all, we will import our avatar
in FBX. We won't need to add join
animation or out arrangement points as
the pose on the size of the avatar
doesn't match with the avatars we have
in MD library. So, we uncheck those
boxes and import the file. Once we have
the avatar in the scene, we open the
avatar editor and go to arrangement tab.
Here we can create new bounding volumes
or arrangement points with the plus
button we have in top of the hierarchy.
If we click there, we will create our
first bounding volume. We change the
name of the volume by double clicking
it.
Next step is to assign it first to the
joints we want it to be oriented. In
case we have a rig, we select the start
joint and the end joint of the rig. Then
we change the width of the volume to an
appropriate measure that can work with
our avatar.
We keep creating those volumes and
assigning them to the different parts of
the body.
When we have all the bounding volumes
that we wanted to create set up, we can
proceed to create the arrangement
points. To create the arrangement
points, click on the plus button.
It will create an arrangement point that
we can assign to a bounding volume. I
will change the naming and then assign
it.
Then we can change the position of the
arrangement point around the volume. You
can use the X or Y options to move it
around or the offset to put it far or
closer to the bounding volume. You can
create all what you need. I will create
two just to show you how to do it for
each bounding volume.
When we finish adding the arrangement
points to the different bounding
volumes, we will finish the setup of our
character by remapping the IK rig in MD.
We go to the IK rig tab and we will
select each part of the body with its
respective bone in our character.
Once we finish, we can set the tose. So
when we move the character, we can
always return to the original position.
We can also use the auto remapping and
let MD link our different bones with the
different parts of our character. It
will be done in a second and after that
we can set our tost and our character
will be finished and ready to use in MD.
And that's all. Thanks for watching this
tutorial. Check our channel and we see
you in the next video.

title: Marvelous Designer 2025.2: Everywear Tutorial (English)
Description: This video is a revised edition of the EveryWear tutorial, introducing its main features and explaining how to use them.
Transcript:
Introduction
Hello everyone, and welcome to the EveryWear tutorial.
EveryWear is a feature that connects creators’ digital garments to various avatars and digital environments.
With EveryWear, creators can easily optimize garments made in CLO or Marvelous Designer
for use in different digital settings such as games, metaverse platforms, and entertainment projects.
In this tutorial, we’ll learn step by step how to use EveryWear for garment fitting, mesh optimization, rigging, UV packing, and texture baking.
Getting Started
Click CONNECT from the main menu at the top to launch EveryWear.
The EveryWear window appears in the upper-right corner of the 2D window,
and you can check the polygon counts of the garment and avatar in the lower-left corner of the 3D window.
EveryWear consists of two main tabs: the Garment tab and the Material tab.
In the Garment tab, you can perform Polygon Optimization and Rigging tasks.
In the Material tab, you can handle UV Packing, Texture Baking, and Material application.
Polygon Optimization
Since the number of meshes and file size supported vary by platform,
you need to optimize the garment’s poly count according to each platform’s requirements.
In the Garment tab, you can optimize the garment’s poly count for the platform of your choice.
Optimize
The number displayed to the right of Garment Polygons in the EveryWear window
represents the total number of meshes in the garment,
including elements such as buttons and trims.
When the garment mesh style is changed to Quad,
Garment Polygons shows the total poly count by adding the number of converted Quad polygons and the remaining Triangles.
Garment Triangles displays the total poly count of the garment converted into the number of Triangles.
In the Avatar section below, you can check the polygon count of the avatar.
You can also view the total polygon count in the lower-left corner of the 3D window.
To optimize the garment’s polygon count,
enter the target polygon number in the empty field next to the Garment section and click the Optimize button.
The garment’s polygons will be automatically optimized to match the entered value.
If you want to optimize each pattern individually,
select the pattern and adjust the Particle Distance value under Property Editor > Simulation Properties to control the mesh counts.
Individual Trim Optimization is useful when button or trim meshes are high-poly.
Select the Button or Trim you want to optimize from the Object Browser,
then go to the bottom of the Property Editor window.
Under Polygon Optimization > Face Count, enter the desired value.
The trim’s polygons will be automatically optimized to match the entered number.
You can further reduce the mesh count of trims by using the Trim Billboarding feature.
Check the Plane box at the bottom to convert the trim into a flat image.
To change the garment’s mesh type to Quad,
select the pattern and choose Quad under Property Editor > Geometry > Mesh Type.
Open the completed garment file after simulation and creation,
then use the Polygon Optimization feature in EveryWear to adjust the garment’s mesh count.
Thickness
Select the pattern to which you want to apply thickness,
then go to Property Editor > Geometry and follow the steps below.
Enter the desired thickness value under Add’l Thickness - Rendering (mm).
The applied thickness can be viewed in the 3D window only when the display mode is set to Thick Textured Surface.(Alt+1)
To clearly view the mesh structure, enable the Show Wireframe feature.(Alt+W)
You can easily toggle it on and off by pressing the Alt+W shortcut key.
In the Extrusion Direction setting, you can define the direction in which thickness is applied.
Selecting Both applies thickness to both the front and back sides of the pattern.
Forward applies thickness to the front side, while Backward applies it to the inner side of the pattern.
You can also specify which surfaces to display based on the normal direction using the Front, Back, and Seam Face checkboxes.
Front Face displays the front side based on the normal direction,
Back Face displays the back side, and Seam Face shows the overlapping surfaces around the seam lines.
Side Geometry
In Side Geometry, you can control the curvature and mesh subdivision of the pattern’s side surface.
Adjust the Curvature value to set the roundness.
Values closer to 100 create a smoother curve,
while values closer to 0 make the surface more angular.
Use the Resolution setting to define the number of subdivisions for the side mesh.
The default value is 6, and it can be set from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 10.
Set ting the value to 0 removes the side mesh entirely.
The Curvature value only takes effect when the Resolution is set to 2 or higher.
You can also apply different Resolution values to each segment by clicking the line with the Edit Pattern tool.
Tip: The Resolution value for all patterns is set to 6 by default.
For mesh optimization, it is recommended to lower the Resolution value below 6
or set it to 0 for patterns that do not require thickness.
Auto Seal
The Auto Seal feature closes open areas such as sleeves or hems to prevent the inside of the garment from being visible.
By filling these openings, you can avoid exposing the garment’s interior when the avatar moves,
improving the overall completeness of the garment.
Click the Auto Seal button to choose between Disc Mode and 3D Pen Mode.
In Disc Mode, you create a disc by placing three points on the pattern, and the curve cut by the disc serves as the guideline.
In 3D Pen Mode, you draw a curve directly on the garment to create a guideline.
It works the same way as the standard 3D Pen tool, and the first and last points must connect to complete the curve.
After creating the guideline, select the direction in which the surface will be generated to apply Auto Seal.
The inner sealed mesh is automatically masked to prevent unnecessary mesh usage.
The area created by Auto Seal can only be viewed in the garment thickness display mode.
If you want to delete it, select and remove the internal line created on the pattern in the 2D window.
Mask Brush
The Mask Brush feature allows you to mask specific areas of the garment so that only the necessary parts are retained,
enabling you to export an optimized garment file.
Click the Brush icon next to Polygon Optimization to enter the Mask Brush tab.
The Front and Back tabs in Mask Brush are based on the 2D pattern window,
while in the 3D window, you can mask both sides simultaneously.
In the Type section, you can choose how to select areas—Brush, Box, or Lasso.
Use Mode to add or remove Mask areas.
Adjust the brush size with Size.
When the Select Enclosed Region option is enabled,
the entire closed area containing the selected point will be automatically masked.
This option is available only when Type is set to Brush.
When the Double Sided Brush option is turned on,
both the front and back sides can be masked simultaneously.
Click Clear All Masks to remove all masks applied to the Front or Back.
Click Reset to restore the Mode and Size settings to their defaults,
or click Exit to close the Mask Brush window and return to the EveryWear window.
Once the Mask Brush window is closed,
the meshes with masked areas will appear as deleted in the 3D window.
Rigging
Rigging is a process in 3D modeling process that creates a skeleton structure composed of joints and bones,
allowing a modeled object to be animated.
In EveryWear, rigging links the garment to the avatar’s joints,
synchronizing their movements so the garment moves naturally with the avatar.
The rigging process also includes weight painting,
which defines how much each part of the garment is influenced by the movement of the avatar’s joints.
This creates a controllable structure that allows the garment and avatar to move smoothly together.
While CLO and Marvelous Designer specialize in realistic cloth simulation and can produce lifelike garment animations,
simulation-based animation tends to have large file sizes, making it inefficient for game environments.
Therefore, in the game industry, rigging is used to synchronize garment and avatar movement in a more optimized way.
EveryWear’s Rigging feature provides an efficient solution for connecting garments and avatars for this purpose.
EveryWear Rigging applies rigging to the garment based on the avatar’s weight information.
The avatar must have joints and be in a human form, and rigging only works when the avatar is in an A-pose or T-pose.
In the Garment tab, click the Apply button under Rigging to automatically rig the garment.
After rigging is applied, the Update and Brush tools become available.
The Target Joint option is used to exclude or remove the weight of specific joints from the rigging target.
If the garment has already been rigged, set the Target Joint and click Update to remove the weight applied to that joint.
Enable Show Avatar Joints to view the avatar’s joint points in the 3D window.
Use the Max Influence Joint option to define the maximum number of joints that can influence each vertex.
Click Switch to Bind Pose to return the avatar to its original pose defined during creation.
This function is independent of the current or recently loaded pose,
and if you switch to Bind Pose before rigging is applied, the current draped shape may be altered.
It is recommended to perform rigging while in Bind Pose, as rigging in a different pose may cause artifacts when adjusting weights.
When using the All Patterns option, all patterns will be rigged or updated.
Using the Selected Patterns option allows you to rig or update only the selected patterns.
For best results, rig all patterns first using the All Patterns option, and then use Selected Patterns for partial adjustments if needed.
After Auto Rigging is complete, you can see that weights have been applied to the garment,
allowing it to move along with the avatar when changing poses.
If you run a Simulation while rigging is active, a warning message will appear.
Selecting Yes will simulate the garment and remove the rigging information,
while selecting No will cancel the simulation and keep the rigging data.
Click the Update button to reapply rigging based on the current state.
When you click the Brush tool, the EveryWear window temporarily closes,
and the Brush tool appears in the upper-right corner of the 3D window.
Use the Weight Brush to perform weight painting.
Weight painting defines how much each joint influences the surrounding vertices, allowing the rigged garment to move naturally with the avatar’s motion.
Through this process, you can achieve realistic and smooth movement.
Although EveryWear’s Rigging feature automatically distributes weights,
you should inspect the garment to ensure that no areas are penetrating the avatar’s body or failing to follow its motion,
and make manual adjustments where needed.
Weight Brush
The Weight Brush offers four Blend Modes: Add, Subtract, Smooth (Single Joint), and Smooth (Multiple Joints).
You can switch between them using the shortcut Ctrl + Tab.
Add increases the weight, Subtract decreases it, and Smooth blends the weight values to make them consistent with the surrounding areas.
In Smooth Brush mode, Single Joint smooths the weight differences between the selected joint and its surrounding vertices.
By pressing Ctrl + Shift and clicking a joint, you can smooth all weights associated with that joint.
Multiple Joints mode applies smoothing to all joints, blending the weights of every joint on each vertex with its neighboring vertices.
Therefore, in multiple joints mode, you can smooth the weights across all areas.
In the brush properties, you can adjust Strength, Size, Focal, and Depth.
Strength controls the intensity of the brush.
Size adjusts the brush radius.
Focal defines the intensity difference between the brush center and its edges, while Depth determines how deep the brush affects the surface.
Click Reset to restore the properties to their default values, and click Exit to close the Brush tool and return to the EveryWear window.
Let’s use the Weight Brush to adjust the weights.
In the 3D window, hold down the Ctrl key and click a joint to view the weights assigned to it.
The weights are displayed in color: red indicates a higher weight value, green represents a medium value, and blue shows a lower value.
Areas without any color have a weight value of 0.
You can use the brush to add, subtract, or smooth weight values.
This can also be performed in the 2D pattern window.
Use the shortcut Shift+X to move joints or apply a preset pose.
This allows you to check if any parts of the garment are penetrating the avatar’s body or not following its movement.
Once you identify areas that need correction, adjust the Blend Mode and brush properties to add or subtract weights as needed.
Hammering
If a specific vertex has a weight value that differs significantly from its surrounding vertices,
you can use the Hammering feature to automatically match it to nearby values.
Hold the Shift key and click the desired vertex to apply the adjustment.
When activated, the mouse cursor changes from a brush to a red dot, indicating vertex recognition.
The Hammering feature is particularly useful for fixing mesh distortion caused by unwanted joint influence in areas such as the armpits, pant hems, or sleeves.
Joint Lock
When you want to limit weight adjustments to a specific area, you can use the Joint Lock feature.
This function is useful when you need to prevent selected joints from being affected during weight editing,
stop unrelated joints from influencing the mesh, or make precise adjustments in complex models.
Locked joints remain unaffected even if you modify weights associated with other joints.
Hold the Alt key and click a joint to apply a lock.
The locked joint will be highlighted in red.
To lock all joints, hold Alt and right-click any joint.
If a joint is already locked, press Alt and click it again to unlock it.
To unlock all joints, hold Alt and right-click.
Copy Symmetric Weights
When patterns are set as symmetrical, you can use the Copy Symmetric Weights feature to copy the weight values from one pattern to its symmetric pattern.
This feature allows you to quickly apply identical weight values, greatly reducing the time needed for weight adjustments.
This feature is available in Weight Brush mode.
First, select the pattern you want to copy weights from in the 2D or 3D window. 
If multiple patterns are selected, the weights of each selected pattern will be copied.
However, if both symmetrical patterns are selected simultaneously, the copy operation will not be executed.
After selecting the pattern, right-click and choose Copy Symmetric Weights to apply the copied weight values to the opposite symmetrical pattern.
Sculpt Brush
Next is the Sculpt Brush.
You can switch to brush mode by pressing the shortcut Ctrl + `.
If the garment is pierced or overlapping, you can use the Sculpt Brush to directly adjust its shape.
The Sculpt Brush has three Blend Modes: Grab, Smooth, and Fix Intersection, which can be switched using Ctrl + Tab.
Additionally, the brush properties are the same as those for the Weight Brush, allowing you to adjust Strength, Size, Focal, and Depth.
The Grab brush is useful for pulling parts of the garment that have penetrated the avatar or for moving overlapping layers on the surface.
Click and drag the desired area, and it will move accordingly without affecting the weight values.
The Smooth brush is used to refine the garment surface or to make jagged and uneven areas appear natural.
Click and drag over the desired area to apply the brush, and the surface will smoothly adjust to match the surrounding shape.
The Fix Intersection brush is used when meshes of the avatar and garment, or between garments, overlap in a way that is difficult to fix with other brushes.
Select the Brush tool, then go to Sculpt Mode → Blend Mode → Fix Intersection.
Adjust the Strength, Size and Depth values, then click and drag to apply it to the model.
Applying the brush this way automatically corrects collisions between the avatar and garment or between garments.
Change the avatar’s pose to check for areas in the garment that penetrate or do not follow correctly.
Use the Weight Brush and Sculpt Brush functions learned so far to make natural adjustments.
Once all rigging and adjustments are complete, click the Exit button to return to the EveryWear window.
UV Packing
Move to the Material tab.
In the Material tab, you can use the UV Packing feature.
This feature automatically arranges the garment’s UVs to prevent overlap and efficiently organizes many UVs at once.
First, in the EveryWear - UV Packing window, set the UV image size and the Seam Size, which defines the spacing between UV pieces.
Clicking the Pack UVs button will briefly close the EveryWear window and open the UV Packing detailed settings window.
In this window, you can configure options related to UV Packing.
Fidelity is an option to set the accuracy of the UVs from 1 to 5.
Higher values closer to 5 place the UVs more accurately according to their original shape, but packing time may increase.
Enabling Fix Scale Ratio allows you to adjust the overall size while maintaining the proportions between UV shells.
Enabling Rotation permits the UV shells to rotate.
Turning on Advanced Placement uses various placement methods to minimize empty space and achieve more efficient packing.
However, higher accuracy may result in longer packing times.
The 0 to 1 option in UV Area places the selected UVs in the default tile at the 0,0 area.
The Selected Tile option allows you to specify a tile manually and pack the selected UVs into that area.
Clicking the Reset button will restore all options to their default values,
and clicking Apply will automatically pack the UVs according to the configured settings.
After configuring all options, clicking Apply will pack all UVs.
If multiple UV tiles are needed for the garment or specific purposes,
you can select the desired pattern in the UV Editor and click Apply to pack them individually.
Once UV packing is complete, click the Exit button to return to the EveryWear window.
Texture Baking
Texture Baking is a feature that generates maps to capture the details of a High Poly model on an optimized model.
The reason for using a Low Poly model for Texture Baking is that Low Poly models have smaller file sizes and are more suitable for optimization.
Additionally, game engines, AR, and other digital platforms often struggle to handle High Poly models.
Using EveryWear’s Texture Baking, you can generate Normal Maps and Ambient Occlusion Maps using only an optimized Low Poly model, without creating a separate High Poly model.
A Normal Map is a texture map commonly used in games and other interactive platforms for real-time rendering,
allowing the surface details of a High Poly model to be represented on a Low Poly model without increasing the polygon count.
An Ambient Occlusion Map is a grayscale texture used in rendering to simulate indirect shadows by tracking light on the surface of a 3D model.
Dark areas represent parts receiving less light, while bright areas indicate well-lit surfaces.
This map predicts shadows on its own and mimics the effect of indirect lighting from the surrounding environment, enhancing realism.
In EveryWear’s Texture Baking window, select Detail Normal Map and Ambient Occlusion Map.
The Ray Sample Count for the AO Map refers to the number of light rays sampled per pixel;
higher values produce more precise results but increase computation time.
After configuring the settings, click the Apply button to generate the maps.
Clicking the Preview button allows you to view the Baked Map in the 3D window.
The strength of the Normal Map can be adjusted by entering a value in the Intensity field or using the slider.
The default value is 100, and it can be set from 0 up to 200.
To delete a generated map, click the trash can icon.
Material List
In the Material List, you can copy existing materials or create new ones, and apply the desired material to selected patterns.
Initially, materials are created according to the number of UV tiles, and you can right-click in the list to rename or delete them.
Clicking the Add button will create a new material, and clicking the Copy button will duplicate the selected material.
Use the Assign button to apply a created material to a pattern,
and the Delete button is enabled only for empty materials that are not assigned to any pattern.
Export
Once all tasks are complete, you can export the file.
Using the Export feature, you can save your garment file directly in FBX format.
Click the Export button at the bottom of the EveryWear window to start the export.
If the export conditions are not met, a warning message will appear.
In that case, resolve the indicated issues and click the Export button again.
When the window for selecting the save location appears, choose your desired folder and file name.
Clicking the Save button will open the Export Options window.
First, set the Platform.
The default is General, and the item will be exported according to the selected platform type.
In this tutorial, we will proceed using General as the reference.
Next, select the options in the Object section.
Garment is selected by default, and in the Thickness option, you can choose either Thin or Thick.
Selecting Thin exports the garment as a single surface without thickness, while selecting Thick applies thickness during export.
Checking the box next to Avatar will export the avatar together with the garment.
In the Texture section, you can choose the types of textures to export.
In the Options section, configure the texture settings.
Selecting Embed Media will include all textures used in the model within the FBX file during export.
In the Graphic Library, choose the format supported by your platform, either OpenGL or DirectX.
Once all selections are complete, click the OK button to start the export.
When the export is finished, a “Success to export file.” message will appear.
Clicking the Reset button will clear all selected options, and clicking the Cancel button will close the Export Options window and return to the EveryWear window.
Save as ZPRJ
Once all tasks are complete, close the EveryWear window.
Saving as a ZPRJ file will store all settings and information applied within the EveryWear window.
Finish
Now we have gone through all the main features of EveryWear.
Follow the steps demonstrated in the video, and if you have any questions or run into any difficulties,
feel free to reach out through the CONNECT community.
Thank you for all your hard work!
We hope you continue to enjoy creating amazing digital garments with EveryWear.

Description: Ready to start animating in Marvelous Designer? This quickstart guide will tell you exactly what you need to know to get started.
Transcript:
Welcome to Marvelous Designer quick
start tutorial. In this video, we'll
guide you through how to use the
animation tools in Marvelous Designer
2025.
There are three ways to open the
animation editor.
First, from the animation tab in the top
main menu.
Second, through the window tab in the
main menu.
And third, by clicking the arrow button
at the very bottom of the interface.
Once opened, you can easily detach the
panel and move it around or close the
editor using the icons at the top right
corner of the panel.
The animation editor is divided into
three key areas. First, the toolbar is
located right at the very top of the
editor. On the far left, you'll find the
simulation record button. Clicking this
will record the garment simulation
together with the avatar's motion, and
the results will be stored in the
timeline.
Next to it are the playback control
buttons. These let you move to the first
frame, step forward frame by frame, or
simply play and pause the animation.
At the center, you'll see the simulation
quality settings. Here you can choose
the desired quality level or enter
values manually for more precise
adjustments.
The higher the value, the longer it
takes to simulate. For most cases, the
animation stable setting should work
fine to begin with.
Below the toolbar is the animation
timeline where you can manage both
garment simulation data and animation
data. Animation data is displayed in
gray while simulation data appears in
red. At the bottom, you'll find the
playback range bar, which lets you
define the start and end frames for
playback. At the top, there is a clamp
that allows you to select a specific
section to play.
Lastly, with the add animation button,
you can add key frames to various
properties like fabric, pattern, avatar,
pin, wind controller, and simulation
property.
Now, let's take a look at the
configurations panel. This panel lets
you adjust how your animation plays
back, including its speed and display
units. First, under play type, you can
choose how the animation will be played.
You can select either frame stepping or
real time.
When it's set to real time and you click
the play button, you'll notice the
simulation runs smoother compared to the
frame stepping option.
Below that, current frame shows the
frame you're currently viewing. Start
frame and end frame define the playback
range. So by setting these values, you
can loop only within that section. Next
is scene time warp. This controls the
playback speed of your animation. A
value of 1.0 plays at the original
speed, while 2.0 plays at half speed,
twice as slow. Increasing values above
one will help you record more frames
during simulation. Once done recording,
you can set it back to one. Display unit
allows you to switch between viewing in
frames or seconds. FPS sets the number
of frames per second for playback.
And lastly, when preserve frames is
checked, the original frames are
maintained and changing the FPS will not
affect them.
When using your custom avatar with
animation, you can import it in FBX,
Olympic or USD format. In this tutorial,
I'll import a custom avatar rigged in
Mixamo without any animation data. If
you are using avatars from platforms
like DOS 3D, Adobe Mixamo, Realusion
Character Creator, or Unreal Engine
Metahuman, just follow my settings.
I set the unit to centimeters Daz Studio
and unchecked all the other options in
the check box.
Next, go to the avatar tab in the main
menu at the top. Click avatar editor and
then open the IK joint tab. As you can
see, the avatar's joints are working in
FK for now. But by clicking auto
mapping, the joints will switch to IK
mode. And if you see the complete sign
at the bottom of the panel, go ahead and
click the set T pose button. Now you can
check that the joints work in IK mode.
And by clicking reset pose, the avatar
will return to its original position.
Now click the library icon at the top
right. Under the avatar tab, open the
mail folder.
There you'll find motion files. I'll
choose walking in place and doubleclick
to apply the motion data to our custom
avatar. Next, click the arrow button to
open the animation editor. Then press
the play button to check the motion. If
the avatar's joints are twisted, you can
use the offset joint feature to correct
their position. Right click on the
applied motion layer and select offset
joint. Then adjust the X-axis value
until the arms are aligned in the
correct position. With the offset joint
feature, you can easily fix misaligned
joints on a custom avatar and adjust it
into the pose you want. Next, to run the
simulation, let's load the garment asset
we've prepared in advance.
Once loaded, change the simulation
quality to animation stable.
Now, let's go ahead and start recording
the animation.
Once the animation recording is
complete, play it back first to make
sure the simulation looks correct. After
confirming, let's use the add animation
feature to apply a wind animation.
First, go to the environment display tab
at the top of the 3D window and check
show wind controller. Next, in the
animation editor, click the add
animation tab and select wind
controller. Now open the newly created
wind controller layer by clicking the
arrow on the left and uncheck unlimited
bound. This way you can directly see and
control the area of the wind and then
click the scale icon at the top right to
expand the range. At this point,
pressing shortcut key5 to switch to the
top view will make adjustments easier.
Once the scaling is done, go back to the
animation editor. Open the transform tab
and then expand the animation editor.
Then open the position and rotation
sections under the transform tab.
Clicking the plus icon here will create
a key frame. If you click the plus icon
next to the X, Y, or Z under rotation,
you can create key frames individually
for each axis.
Now move the timeline cursor to a new
frame.
Then change the position of the wind
controller and click the key frame icon
in the transform tab to create a key
frame all at once. In the same way, move
forward about 30 frames. Adjust the wind
controller's position and create another
key frame. Repeat this process to build
your animation. As a tip, if you turn on
the auto keying button at the top of the
animation editor, key frames will be
created automatically whenever you move
the wind controller, making the workflow
much easier.
Once you finish setting the key frames,
let's change the interpolation of those
key frames and see the difference it
makes. Select all the key frames you
created by dragging over them and then
right click. By default, the
interpolation is set to linear. This
time let's change it to constant and see
the difference. With constant the
transition between key frames is not
smooth. Instead it suddenly jumps. Now
drag to select all the key frames again.
Right click and change the interpolation
to cubic. With cubic the controller's
motion accelerates gradually at the
start and slows down at the end.
I'll set the interpolation back to
linear since I want the wind to flow at
a uniform speed throughout.
Now that all key frames are set, let's
activate the wind. Go back to frame zero
and press the shortcut key3 to switch
from top view to 3/4 view. Then click
the record button.
Great, the recording is complete. Let's
press the play button to see the result.
As you can see, when unlimited bound is
unchecked, the wind only affects the box
area defined by the wind controller.
Next, let's take a look at the video
capture feature. At the top right side
of the animation editor toolbar, you'll
find the video capture button. By using
this feature, you can export the
simulation recorded in the 3D viewport
as a video file for review.
Lastly, if you want to export the
recorded simulation data itself, go to
the top menu and select file arrow
export. From there, you can choose
between formats like FBX, umbic or USD
to output the simulation data. Thank you
for watching.

Transcript:
Welcome to Marvelous Designer quick
start tutorial. In this video, we will
learn about Marvelous Designer modular
library and autofitting tool set. The
modular library can be turned on and off
from the main menu window
menu.
Right click on the top tab of each
window to open and close windows
corresponding to the types of central

library corresponds to the side window,

side window popup menu.
You can close the modular library by
selecting modular library from the
right-click menu on the top tab of the
modular library window.
There is a window minimize arrow on the
upper right of the modular library
window
and a window detach button on the upper
left.
When detaching a window, you can also
detach it by clicking and dragging the
tab of the window.
When you launch modular library, there
are three groups by default, kids, men,
and women.
Double click women to open it and you
will see category folders such as basic
shirts, bottoms and button-downs.
Doubleclick basic shirts to open it. You
will see styles such as drop shoulder,
wriglland, and set in which are sub
menus of that category. Doubleclick drop
shoulder to open it. The block types for
each part of the garment will appear.
Additionally, styles belonging to the
same category will be displayed at the
top. Clicking on each style will display
the blocks for that style below.
This time we will select the
button-downs category under women.
Select long sleeve.
The blocks are configured differently
depending on the garment, but they
usually consist of front body, back
body, sleeves, collar, etc.
Let's configure the garment by selecting
the blocks one by one. Double clicking
each block adds it to the 3D window and
2D pattern window. Double clicking on
the same block will replace the
previously loaded block with the
selected block. Select each block to
complete the garment.

the sewing lines will be automatically
created. In this way, the modular
library allows you to quickly and easily
create garments using blocks.

other styles, you can load the block to
construct the garment.

with each other. The blocks, styles,
categories, and groups used in the
modular library can be customized

more details, please refer to the
modular library tutorial in the
description.
Now, let's load the avatar and try
dressing it using the modular library.
First, prepare a male avatar. Select
men, button-downs, and short sleeve from

Select the desired block from block
types such as front body and back body.

block to replace it.

the same block type in a different
style.
Let's take a look at autofitting, a
feature that allows you to dress your

avatars. For the autofitting feature to
work, both the avatar and the garment
must have fitting suit information.
First, let's create a fitting suit for
custom avatar. For reference, the
avatars provided by Marvelous Designer
include fitting suit information.

automatically create a fitting suit. As
an example, let's import an FBX avatar.

autocreate fitting suit menu.
You can check the avatar's fitting suit
information by selecting show avatar
fitting suit in avatar display.

modify fitting suits in avatar editor.

Select the fitting suit tab to display
the existing fitting suit. The purple
reference line and the fitting suit
preview patterns before simulation are
displayed in gray. If you did not create
a fitting suit when importing the
avatar, you can use the autocreate
fitting suit menu to create one
automatically.

reference line and then select the item
to recreate it. Alternatively, if you
create a new line while the reference
line is selected, the existing line will
be automatically replaced by the new
line. Reference lines are created by
clicking three points, similar to when
creating circumference measure avatar
lines. Until version 2025.0,
the direction of reference lines was
indicated as L based on the user's
perspective. But starting from version
2025.1,
it is indicated as R based on the avatar
in the 3D window.
Once all reference lines are created,
click drape fitting suit to simulate the
fitting suit.
Once the fitting suit is put on, save it
as an AVT file along with the avatar.
Now let's load the garment and run
autofitting. Load the garment for the
kid avatar which is a different size
from the male avatar. Turn on the show
garment fitting suit option in garment
display. The garment fitting suit will
be displayed in red on the kid's
garment. After putting on the garment on
the avatar with the avatar fitting suit.
When you save the garment, the
information of the fitting suit is also
saved with the garment and displayed in
red. When both the avatar fitting suit
and garment fitting suit exist, you can
use the autofitting menu. Since the
garment must be in the same position as
the garment fitting suit, we will return
the garment to its original position.
Click the autofitting tool in the
toolbar.
After making the necessary settings in
the autofitting dialogue, select okay.
Starting with Marvelous Designer 2025.1,
you can use the maintain topology menu
to execute autofitting while maintaining
the topology of the existing garment.
The more vertices the garment has, the
slower the autofitting speed may be.
When executed, the garment fitting suit
is aligned with the avatar fitting suit
and the garment size is also adjusted
and worn.
Next, let's take a look at the
redrarrape 3D arrangement feature. When
you click this tool, the garment fitting
suit is adjusted to match the avatar
fitting suit and the garment is worn
similar to autofitting. However, the
difference from autofitting is that
while autofitting adjusts the garment
size to match the avatar's size and
transforms it accordingly, the
redrarrape 3D arrangement function only
applies the garment to the character
without altering its size. Therefore,
during simulation, the garment is
applied tightly. This concludes our
overview of the autofitting function and
the redrarrape 3D arrangement function.

Transcript:
UI
improvement. The user interface has been
completely redesigned with a cleaner,
more intuitive layout. You can now
freely detach, dock, and rearrange
windows. You can also save and load your
own custom layouts.
The library has also been updated with
larger icons and a streamlined layout
for easier
browsing. You can always switch back and
forth between the original library and
the new library by clicking the icon on
the bottom left corner of the
library. The icons in the toolbar are
bigger and easier to locate, and the
sculpt tool has been relocated to the
toolbar for easier access.
Navigation in the object browser has
been greatly improved, making it much
more accessible and easier to use. You
could easily toggle between scene,
fabric, graphic, buttons, button hole,
top stitch, puckering and
trims. We also have a library icon in
the object browser. You can directly
import various asset from the connect
asset
store. Key frame
animation. Now you can add animations
for different elements like fabric,
pattern pieces, avatars, pins, wind, and
simulation settings. Right from the add
animation
menu, you can now animate fabric
properties like base color and material
changes. Just turn on auto keying and
start tweaking. Key frames will be added
automatically. Next up, pattern
animation. You can change the fabric
used on individual pattern pieces mid
animation. Renaming your pattern parts
helps when controlling over added layers
in the animation editor.
Pin animation lets you control when
cloth pins attach or detach. Perfect for
scenes like towels flying off hangers or
receipts falling from moving
hands. Key framing wind got so much
easier. Move and rotate the wind
controller as your scene plays out and
adjust the wind strength over time for
realistic motion.
Lastly, you can key frame simulation
settings like gravity and air
damping. Make sure to switch to custom
simulation quality and you're good to
go. Quad mesh
improvement. The quad mesh algorithm has
been significantly improved for cleaner
and more accurate topology. You can view
this by turning on show wireframe in the
garment rendering style panel and
switching the mesh type to quad
optimized. Compared to
2024, the new version creates much
cleaner, better aligned quad meshes,
even on basic garments like a t-shirt.
When applied to more complex garments
like a dress with folds and pleats, the
new algorithm preserves details and
shape while improving mesh
structure. First strand in 3D
window. A brand new first strand
material type has been added to fabrics,
piping, and bindings. First strands are
visible in both the 3D window and
quality
render and can be exported with USD
files for use in other 3D
applications. The fur strand display
comes in cylinder, plane or line styles.
You can customize fur using fur presets
and tweak its
shape. Fur parameters and fur shape can
be adjusted to your desire. You can also
play with your custom texture maps for
realistic clumping and
design side and back UV expansion. You
can now expand of your garment mesh for
better texturing control. Make sure to
switch to thick textured surface mode in
order to see the side
UVs. Go to window in the main menu and
click UV editor. Select your UVs and
enable side face or backface UV
expansion in the property editor.
These options generate new UV shells for
the inner and side surfaces. To export
with expanded UVs, make sure unified UV
coordinates PNG is checked in the OBJ
export
settings. Import the result into tools
like Substance 3D Painter and you'll see
clean, nonstretched UVs across all
surfaces. IK joint mapping. A brand new
IK joint mapping allows you to apply
marvelous designers poses and motions to
external FBX avatars as long as they
share the same IK joint structure. It
works with avatars from platforms like
Daz 3D, Maxamo, Character Creator, and
even
Metahuman. Import your Tpose FBX avatar
and go to IK joint mapping tab. In the
avatar editor, you can map joints
manually by selecting each required bone
or let MD handle it with auto
mapping. Once mapping is complete, click
set to pose. If reset pose activates,
you're good to go. Now you can apply
poses and animations from Marvelous
Designer Library to your custom avatar
with
ease. Autocon convert to motion. You can
easily import motion files from external
platforms like Mixamo and apply them to
the default avatar and your custom
avatar. Download any FBX animation files
from Mixamo
first. In Marvelous Designer, go to
avatar and click autoconvert to motion.
Select the avatar type and load your FBX
file.
Click convert to turn it into an MTN
motion file. Once done, save the file.
Now you can apply this MTN motion file
to the marvelous designer default
avatars and you can also apply it to
your custom IK joint mapped avatars.
Modular
library. The new modular library unifies
the old configurator and editor into one
intuitive panel. You can now manage all
garments using a simple
structure. You can click the arrow to
hide or show the window on the left
side. In the previous version, blocks
were registered in the modular editor
and then used in the modular
configurator. Now blocks can be
registered directly within the modular
library. The modular library follows a
folder structure of group, category,
style, block. This structure makes it
convenient to organize and manage
designs by style. When you click the
plus button at the top of the style
list, the group style by line menu
appears. By selecting this option, a new
folder called line is added between
basic shirt category and style and the
existing styles will be grouped under
the line. To register a garment from the
3D window as a block, you need to
sequentially create and register folders
according to this structure. Just like
the previous modular configurator,
double clicking a block will instantly
add the associated patterns to the
scene. New library
window. The library window is now fully
detachable, letting you manage your
workspace with more flexibility. With
one click, you can switch between the
older and new library views to suit your
preference.
You can browse both built-in assets and
connect assets with a toggle to view
free or paid items
easily. Integrated closet allows you to
import projects directly from the cloud
and keep everything in
sync. Finding and applying asset is now
smoother than ever.
You can also create your own custom
library tabs. A big improvement over the
previous all-in-one
system. Adding personal folders and
organizing your assets is now simple and
efficient. Schematic render. The new
schematic render feature is now
available in the render menu. It turns
your 3D garments into simple, clean 2D
line drawings with a stylized tonel-like
feel.
You can adjust the line thickness for
different parts like the silhouette,
seam lines, internal lines, and top
stitch
lines. You could also change the color
of your lines, giving you full control
over the look. It's a great way to
clearly see the garment's pattern and
design details at a glance compared to a
regular 3D
render. With format background, you can
set a green screen background in one
click. Then just hit video capture to
record your scene. It's an easy way to
create videos you can reuse in
presentations, promos, or add custom
backgrounds with chroma key. Two-way
zippers. You can now use two-way
zippers. Just click on the zipper or
puller. Then go to the property editor
on the
right. Under the type option, select
two-way to enable it.
You can also change the direction to
either bottom to bottom or head to head
depending on how you want the zipper to
open. OBJ zipper teeth with preset. We
now support zipper teeth as OBJ through
the teeth type
option. Depending on your needs, you can
either use an optimized texture version
for better performance or a highdetail
OBJ version for more visual accuracy.
Avatar editor improvement. All avatar
related features are now gathered in one
place, the avatar
editor. Create fitting suit, which was
previously in the 3D toolbar, has also
been relocated to the avatar
editor. This makes managing and working
with avatars much more
efficient. Animation with trim
simulation. You can now attach trims
using tack instead of glue for more
stable
control. Use the 3D window and 2D
pattern window together when placing
trims. This lets you position them more
intuitively and accurately exactly where
you want
them. Trims can now be included in
simulation recordings. To get smoother
and more accurate results, apply scene
time warp to your motion data.
This stretches the frame intervals and
allows for more precise simulation
recording. Try adding your custom trim,
apply animation data, and record the
simulation to see it in
action. Autofitting
improvement. The autofitting feature has
been improved. Now you can load an
additional garment and apply autofitting
without affecting the previous one.
This makes using autofitting more
convenient and flexible than ever. Auto
seal. A new auto seal feature has been
added to the everywhere tab under the
connect menu. With auto seal, you can
easily fill open areas in your garment
with just a few
clicks. Using disk option is an easy way
to go, but you can be more detailed and
specific using 3D pen option.
It's perfect for closing unnecessary
gaps and preparing your asset for final
export. After sealing, you can also bake
textures to optimize and manage your
assets more efficiently.

DAZ Studio and turn off the option for
